articles.title: Myanmar leader breaks diplomatic isolation on first official visit to Thailand since coup
articles.summary: The military leader has been barred from western countries and accused of crimes against humanity.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
The BBC's Jonathan Head explains what the meeting between the leaders means By Jonathan Head South East Asia correspondent 
- Published 6 August 2026 
Myanmar's military leader Min Aung Hlaing has arrived on an official visit to Thailand, his first since he launched the coup that ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021. 
The coup ignited a civil war, which has killed thousands of people and wrecked the economy. 
Min Aung Hlaing, who was already subject to sanctions over his involvement in the mass expulsion of Muslim Rohingyas in 2017, has been an international pariah, barred from western countries and accused of crimes against humanity. 
He was declared president in April and left his position as military commander, following an election which was widely condemned for being neither free nor fair. 
The main opposition parties were barred from taking part, and there was no voting at all in large areas of Myanmar controlled by armed insurgents, ensuring that the military's own party now dominates the new parliament. 
Min Aung Hlaing has been barred from attending meetings of the Association of South East Asian Nations (Asean) over his refusal to implement a five-point consensus which he and other Asean member states signed in 2021. It required the Myanmar military to de-escalate violence and start negotiations with opposition groups. 
Some Asean states, in particular Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore, want to see more concessions made by the military in Myanmar to ease the humanitarian crisis there and end the civil war before full diplomatic contact can be restored. 
However, Thailand is pursuing what it calls "calibrated re-engagement" with the regime in Myanmar, arguing that because they share a 2,400 km border they need to be talking to each other at the highest levels of government to address issues like transnational crime. 
That diplomatic engagement by Thailand is moving quickly this week, and looks very much like business as usual. 
Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome by the Thai prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul. He will be attending an official dinner, meeting the leaders of both houses of the Thai parliament, and presiding over a Thai-Myanmar business forum to boost the economic ties between the two countries. 
On Thursday evening, the two leaders released a joint statement that pointedly avoided any mention of Asean's concerns over Myanmar's failure to honour the 2021 consensus, and barely mentioned the civil war at all. 
The main focus was on rebuilding economic ties, which is something the Thai business community wants and managing border issues. 
There was a lot of references to co-operation on security, something that the Thai military, which has significant influence over Thai policy towards Myanmar, wants. 
The statement has no hint of any Thai concerns over the disastrous costs of the civil war, although Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow did tell journalists that Thailand wants the violence to be reduced and to see both sides in the conflict show a willingness to negotiate. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Min Aung Hlaing has been an international pariah, barred from western countries and accused of crimes against humanity 
Thailand's decision closely follows what Myanmar's two largest neighbours, China and India, have done after the election. 
Both have recognised the new government and invited Min Aung Hlaing for official visits soon after he became president. 
China's support for the embattled military regime in Myanmar has been critical, helping it turn the tide on the battlefield and recapture some of the territory it had lost to armed opposition groups. 
But the decision by Thailand, a democracy and a founder member of Asean, to give Min Aung Hlaing such a high-profile visit is attracting a lot of criticism. 
"The Thai government continues to lend the junta false legitimacy through its ongoing diplomatic engagements," said the campaigning group Justice for Myanmar. 
"Min Aung Hlaing's visit reflects Thailand's failed policy of 'calibrated re-engagement' with the military junta, which will only prolong the ongoing suffering of the people of Myanmar."

articles.title: 'Your legacy will live forever': Nepal mourns climber Nirmal Purja
articles.summary: Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed some of the country's best mountaineers.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Students and staff at Purja's former school lit candles in commemoration of him By Koh Ewe 
- Published 3 August 2026 
Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed all 10 members of an expedition on Pakistan's Broad Peak, six of whom were Nepalese. 
Among them was Nirmal Purja, also known as Nims, a British-Nepali climber most known for climbing the world's 14 tallest peaks in just over six months. 
His death has sent shockwaves through the global mountaineering community and through Nepal, where he is a celebrated figure for giving a spotlight to Nepali climbing guides. 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah was among those who paid tribute, saying his "history of courage, dedication and contribution will always remain inspiring". 
In a moving tribute on Facebook, Purja's brother Kamal wrote: "I feel as though I have lost my whole world. My brother was not only my younger brother - he was my heart." 
"Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added. 
At the Small Heaven School in Chitwan district, near Kathmandu, which Purja had once attended, students and staff lit candles and mourned his death. 
Sarbagya Paudel, one of the students at the vigil, said Purja's "bravery has set a great example for our school. Not only has he made our school proud, but he has also brought pride to Nepal". 
Purja is still fondly remembered by those who had known him from his schooling days. Shailendra Baral, his school hostel supervisor, told AFP that as a young boy Purja had been "fearless and committed to achieving something". 
"He was honest and an obedient student, which made us happy. We found courage in him even when he was a child." 
Bahadur Panta, Purja's school friend, said he had prayed for the mountaineer through "sleepless nights" after news broke of his disappearance. 
"It was not only me and my friends. I think people all over the world who knew him... prayed for him. But it was his fate, no one could avoid it," he told AFP. 
Social media was also awash with tributes to Purja, with many saying that Nepal was in mourning and that the country had lost a "legend" and "many great climbers". 
"Their legacy will live on," said one comment. 
Purja was catapulted into international stardom after his journey was documented in a 2021 Netflix documentary. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Bahadur Panta was a friend of Purja's in school 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
He was among dozens that gathered at the Small Heaven school in Chitwan 
Among his 10-member expedition on Broad Peak, there were six Nepali climbers. The other four climbers were from the US, China, Oman, Pakistan. 
They had gone missing after being caught in an avalanche last Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak. 
Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit. 
Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives. 
Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. 
Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military. 
But as he became more famous, troubling allegations emerged about his conduct. 
In 2024, a New York Times article detailed sexual allegations two women made against Purja. One alleged that he had sexually assaulted her in a hotel room in 2023 and another said he had grabbed and propositioned her while guiding her on an expedition to K2 in 2022. He denied these claims through his lawyer. 
- 
Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche 
- Published 4 days ago 
- 
Who is Nirmal Purja, the famed mountaineer killed in Broad Peak avalanche? 
- Published 4 days ago 
But while Purja may be the most recognisable face, he was not the only famed climber in the disaster-hit expedition on Broad Peak. The 10-member team also consisted of big names in Nepal's climbing community. 
There was Pur Bahadur Gurung - also known as Yukta - who summitted Everest 10 times. In 2024, he was part of the team that discovered a century-old shoe on the world's tallest peak, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on Everest with George Mallory in 1924. 
"Standing with you on the summit of Mount Everest is a memory I will cherish forever," fellow mountaineer and guide Uttam Lapraki wrote in a tribute to Yukta on social media. 
"The Himalayas have lost one of their finest sons, but your courage, kindness, and legacy will continue to inspire generations of climbers." 
Another member of the team, Kili Pemba Sherpa, was part of a historic 2021 expedition that summitted K2, the world's second-highest peak, in winter. That expedition was made up of all Nepali climbers, including Purja. 
Imagine Nepal, an expedition company where Kili Pemba worked as a guide, wrote on Instagram that he had "stood with us from the very beginning, from the days we first started climbing together". 
"He was humble in every way and never tired of helping climbers when they needed him. He was a foundation of our team and a part of every summit we have ever celebrated."

articles.title: Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant
articles.summary: A New Mexico judge ordered the Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp parent company to pay another $567m for the way it has harmed children.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has seen his company face an increasing number of lawsuits over child safety By Kali Hays Technology reporter 
- Published 7 August 2026, 00:34 BST Updated 36 minutes ago 
A US judge in New Mexico on Thursday ordered Meta to pay another $567m (£421m) for its failure to warn the public about dangers its platforms posed to children, marking the largest ruling against the company over child safety. 
Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the social media giant is a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution and that it must put the money in a fund aimed at reducing future harms. 
The ruling is in addition to $375m in fines Meta was already ordered to pay in the case, for a total of $942m. 
Judge Biedscheid compared Meta to a factory, with advertising and content as its product and "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children to be the pollution that must be abated". 
A spokesman for Meta, which owns and operates Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, said Thursday: "We disagree with the ruling and will appeal." 
"We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts." 
Regarding the earlier $375m verdict in the case, Meta had said it intended to appeal the ruling and gave a similar explanation. It was the first time that a state had successfully sued Meta over child safety issues. 
Meta is currently facing thousands of lawsuits in the US over similar issues. In addition to the New Mexico rulings, Meta earlier this year lost a case in Los Angeles making similar claims. 
The New Mexico case stems from a 2023 lawsuit brought by attorneys for the State of New Mexico, arguing Meta should be held liable for the way in which its platforms endangered children and exposed them to sexually explicit material and contact with sexual predators. 
In the first phase of the trial, Meta was found to have repeatedly violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act as its recommendation algorithms essentially "steered" young users toward harmful content and contacts. 
Recommendation algorithms are the tools that Meta uses to automatically curate the content a user sees on its platforms. 
In ruling on this second phase of the trial, Judge Biedscheid found that Meta's harms reached the level of "public nuisance", or an issue of health and safety that has become so widespread it is negatively impacting a general public. 
In addition to being the largest fine Meta has received over child safety issues, the ruling also appears to be the first time that a social media company has been deemed a public nuisance. 
"Just as noxious pollution produced by the factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms and, instead, migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world and create a common, societal burden on and harm to the affected children and their families and schools, as well as hospitals and law enforcement," the judge wrote. 
The fund that Meta has been ordered to create will be used to pay for efforts to mitigate "the wide-ranging impacts of the harm", Judge Biedscheid said. 
A vast majority of the money, totaling $420m, will go towards treatment of harms Meta's platforms have already caused, through the funding of "appropriate clinical or other behavioral health programs and professionals," according to the order. 
Another chunk of the money will go towards training around awareness and prevention, including for teachers and health professionals on how to deal with social media harms against children. 
The judge also ordered Meta to enact other measures, including ensuring that no account of a user under age 18 is recommended to an adult and that no adult can message an underage user, banning the sending or receiving of nudity by underage users and enacting a "1-strike policy for adult users who engage in child sexual exploitation." 
In addition, Meta was ordered to: 
- 
Eliminate "like" counts for users under 18 
- 
Ban push notifications for such users every day between 10:00 PM to 7:00 AM and to ban such notifications during the typical school year between 8:00 AM to 3:00 PM, except on weekends 
- 
Implement a mandatory usage limit for such users of 90 cumulative hours per month across Instagram and Facebook, or about three hours per day 
Next week, another major trial against Meta begins in California. Nearly three dozen US states' attorneys general are suing the company for violating child privacy laws.

articles.title: Trump imposes 15% tariff on key chip material to counter China
articles.summary: The move aims to counter Chinese producers, which hold a monopoly in the global polysilicon production.
articles.full_text:
Image source, VCG via Getty Images Image caption, 
China is the world's biggest producer of polysilicon, a key material used in making chips and solar panels By Osmond Chia Business reporter 
- Published 7 August 2026, 01:44 BST Updated 26 minutes ago 
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that imposes a 15% tariff on imported products made from polysilicon, a crucial material used in semiconductors and solar panels. 
The order also set minimum import prices on polysilicon and related products. It comes after a national security investigation into the production of the material overseas. 
The move is intended to help protect US manufacturers as they face increasing competition from China's chip industry - a key source of friction between the world's two largest economies. 
The Chinese embassy in Washington said the move "seriously disrupts" trade between the two countries and Beijing will act to protect its companies. 
Washingtom is "abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses," the embassy said, adding that protectionism will not make the US more competitive. 
Trump said in the order , external that he had accepted recommendations by Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to set minimum import prices as well as a 15% tariff on polysilicon and related imports. 
The measures are due to take effect in December. 
The US will also offer incentives to boost domestic production, it added. 
For decades, the US has allowed "foreign firms to weaken United States producers in the polysilicon sector," said Trump, who has long advocated for the use of tariffs to protect American jobs and boost the economy. 
The material is critical in military equipment and electronics, yet imports have led to the US' share of global polysilicon production to fall from 50% in 2005 to less than 2% in 2024, Trump said. 
China holds a near monopoly on the production of polysilicon. 
The order is likely to benefit Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker Chemie, which are the main producers of the material in the US. 
The production of computer chips is central to the race between the US and China to develop artificial intelligence (AI). Washington and Beijing have also been locked in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which has been on hold since May 2025. 
Analysts quoted by Chinese state media outlet Global Times said the new tariff marks the latest escalation in Washington's efforts to limit China's role in critical technology supply chains. 
The move follows other US restrictions on the imports of drones, humanoid robots and other tech products from China. 
China announced a range of countermeasures this week, including tighter export controls on drones. Beijing also launched a national security review into imported printers and copiers.

articles.title: TikTok star Sydney Towle, who shared her cancer journey online, dies aged 26
articles.summary: Towle was known for chronicling her hopes and struggles as a young person living with cancer.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images for Miami Swim Week: The Shows Image caption, 
Towle recently fulfilled her dream of modelling at Miami Swim Week By Grace Eliza Goodwin 
- Published 6 August 2026 
Sydney Towle, a popular social media influencer who shared her experience living with a rare, aggressive form of cancer, has died at the age of 26. 
Towle's family announced her death, from complications related to bile duct cancer that had spread to other parts of her body, on her social media accounts on Thursday. 
"Syd went peacefully last night after an almost three-year-long battle with cholangiocarcinoma," her brother Austin said in a video message, alongside their mother, on TikTok. 
Towle, who was moved to hospice care earlier this week, had over a million followers on TikTok and over 200,000 on Instagram. 
She spent the last three years chronicling her daily life as a young person going through chemotherapy and living with cancer, with all its hopes, joys and struggles. She had been living in New York City at the time of her death. 
"We are so proud of how hard Sydney fought and for sharing her journey with so many people," Towle's family said in a statement. 
"She wanted to raise awareness for rare cancers and was passionate about promoting self-advocacy. We will continue her legacy and honour her in every way we can." 
Following the announcement of her death, thousands of followers posted messages on Towle's social media accounts paying tribute to her and sending well wishes to her family. 
"Sweet angel. Fly high," actress Alyssa Milano commented. "Praying for all who loved her. She is really something special." 
"You were such a bright light and will be missed," one person wrote on Instagram, while another said: "How lucky we all are to have found you on the internet. Thank you for sharing yourself and your story." 
Image source, Sydney Towle/Instagram 
In May, Towle posted a series of videos from the hospital where she was receiving treatment for complications related to her cancer. 
She shared that her cancer had spread to her peritoneum, a membrane that lines the abdominal and pelvic cavities and protects internal organs. 
On 19 May, she posted a video of herself, sitting beside her mother in the hospital, in which she said her oncologist had told her he would no longer treat her cancer, recommending she begin end-of-life care. Towle said she would not accept this and vowed to continue fighting, choosing instead to switch to another specialist. 
Despite her illness, she expressed fervent optimism and joy for life on her social media accounts. She often posted videos of herself dancing, getting ready, and having fun with friends. 
She recently fulfilled her dream of modelling, walking in a swimsuit for The Chemo Club x Post Swim show at Miami Swim Week. 
"Rich in life because my friends choose to spend a Saturday fundraising for cancer research," Towle wrote in a post in March. 
"Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry's, watch your favourite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn't make it a bad life," Towle wrote in another post last year. 
Towle was not shy about showing her stomach, where she had a hepatic artery pump implanted, on social media. 
"I have only recently started seeing the resilience and beauty in this body," she wrote in a post last year, alongside photos of herself in a swimsuit. "Scars that remind me of how far I've come. And I'm reminded that dreams only end when you allow them to."

articles.title: US Senate committee votes to hold Fauci in contempt over Covid hearing
articles.summary: The committee will now refer him for possible prosecution for refusing to answer questions about his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment in showdown with Republican lawmakers on 29 July By Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter 
- Published 6 August 2026 
A US Senate committee has voted to hold former top health official Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions during a hearing examining his handling of the Covid-19 pandemic. 
The vote - which fell along party lines - clears the way for the committee to refer the case to the justice department for potential prosecution for failing to comply with a congressional subpoena. 
It remains unclear whether the department will pursue the case. 
During his testimony last week, Fauci invoked his constitutional right against self-incrimination more than 100 times, arguing that Kentucky Senator Rand Paul was trying to put him "behind bars". 
In a statement following the vote, Fauci's lawyer called it a "crude political stunt" being conducted to "punish Dr Fauci for exercising his constitutional right". 
The origins of the pandemic have been a matter of strong debate in the US, including between President Donald Trump, who was in office when it began in 2020, and public health officials, including Fauci. 
Senator Rand Paul has for years accused Fauci of attempting to hide its origins and of funding a research lab in the Chinese city of Wuhan, where some believe the pandemic began with a lab-leak. 
Most scientists believe that exposure to an infected animal is a more likely origin for the pandemic. 
Former President Joe Biden gave Fauci a pre-emptive pardon on his last day in office in 2025, protecting him from federal prosecution for his actions between 2014 and 2025. 
But Fauci could still face charges for anything after that date, including contempt of Congress. He could also face state or local charges that are not covered by the pardon. 
"The chair directed Anthony Fauci to answer. He refused," Kentucky Republican Rand Paul said ahead of the vote. "That is what we are voting on today — not his opinions, not his policies, not anything he said from the podium six years ago. " 
"We are voting on whether a witness who has received the benefit of a federal pardon can be ordered by this committee to answer questions and then defy that order without consequence," he added. 
The Top Democrat on the committee, Michigan Senator Gary Peters, defended Fauci, accusing Paul of a "rushed investigation" and a "yearslong campaign" to prosecute Fauci. 
Fauci has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and last week accused Paul of having an "obvious obsession" with prosecuting him. 
"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something - anything - that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, 'behind bars'," Fauci said. 
Paul, the committee's Republican chairman, bypassed a full senate vote on the contempt resolution saying he did not "want to waste time" going through the procedure. 
Normally, contempt resolutions passed by the committee go to the full Senate, where they require a 60-vote majority. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member Senate. 
In a statement quoted by US news outlets, Dr Fauci's lawyer, David Schertler, called on the Senate to "reject Senator Paul's meritless and politically-motivated contempt resolution". 
"For years, Senator Paul has proclaimed to anyone who would listen that Dr Fauci should be prosecuted and put in prison," Schertler added. "Dr Fauci has committed no crime — and Senator Paul knows it." 
Schertler had previously argued that he believes that the former top health official is on "solid legal ground" going forward, adding that Paul "may be a doctor, but he is not a lawyer". Paul worked as an eye surgeon until he got elected to the US Senate in 2010. 
"We are completely confident that Dr Fauci has a valid Fifth Amendment privilege here and is on solid legal ground in asserting it," attorney David Schertler said in an e-mail to CBS, the BBC's US partner, last week. 
Taking the Fifth is not an admission of guilt - it is designed to protect individuals against coercion, mistakes, and unfair shifting of the burden to provide proof of wrongdoing. 
Contempt prosecutions - and convictions - are rare. 
In 2024, former Trump allies Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro were both convicted of contempt and sentenced to jail sentences, marking the first convictions since the 1980s.

articles.title: DR Congo river boat under quarantine for Ebola after five deaths
articles.summary: The health minister says all the passengers are being screened as a precautionary measure.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The Yingfeng 2 was intercepted on the Congo River before it could reach Kinshasa By Emery Makumeno BBC Africa ,  Reporting from Kinshasa 
- Published 6 August 2026 
Congolese authorities are carrying out Ebola and cholera screening for all 255 passengers aboard a boat intercepted on the Congo River. 
The Yingfeng 2 - operated by a Chinese company - was halted near Bende Bende port, some 65km (40 miles) upstream from the capital, Kinshasa. 
Health Minister Roger Kamba said screening was being carried out as a precautionary measure after a passenger with fever and diarrhoea, who had left the boat in Mongala Province , died in hospital. A further two adults, a three-year-old child and a newborn have also died. 
Teams from the health ministry and the World Health Organization (WHO) have boarded the boat and set up a mobile lab to conduct tests. 
"For now, no-one has tested positive, and it is likely no one will be positive after 21 days of incubation has elapsed," Kamba told reporters. 
He also said that the vessel had departed from Mongala in north-western DR Congo 22 days ago, where there have been no Ebola cases, contrary to earlier reports. 
The passenger had already been travelling on the boat for some days before being taken to Pimu health zone for treatment, still in Mongala. 
- 
Why Uganda is winning the battle against Ebola as virus spreads in DR Congo 
- Published 5 days ago 
The boat travelled more than 1,700km downstream towards Kinshasa before being intercepted. 
Security services have been instructed to quarantine the Yingfeng  2 offshore in line with WHO standards to prevent potential spread of the virus into the capital. Public health teams remain on standby to act once the boat is secured. 
The country has been grappling with its 17th Ebola outbreak since 15 May. It has been caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, which had not been seen for more than a decade. 
There are no drug treatments that specifically target Bundibugyo, nor does it have a vaccine, although the first human trials for one are currently under way in the UK. 
Three months since the outbreak was declared, infections and deaths continue to rise. 
Official figures show that there have been 3,973 confirmed cases and 1,801 deaths - the second deadliest Ebola outbreak. 
There are currently more than 17,000 people under monitoring after coming into contact with Ebola cases, 674 patients in isolation or treatment across five provinces, and 776 recoveries, according to authorities. 
In Kinshasa, preparations for a possible Bundibugyo response are intensifying, with surveillance and rapid-response capacity being reinforced at Maluku, the city's main entry point. 
Officials have reiterated that the measures are precautionary, but they underline the gravity of the situation.

articles.title: Livestreamer's murder raises questions over relations between Mexico's creators and cartels
articles.summary: The murder of content creator César Gastélum on Tuesday raises questions about why influencers are coming under attack.
articles.full_text:
Image source, César Gastélum/YouTube By Daniel Pardo Mexico correspondent, BBC News Mundo 
- Published 6 August 2026 
The killing of a young influencer, caught on camera as he was livestreaming in Mexico's Sinaloa state, has raised questions about possible links between content creators and criminal cartels in this violence-wracked part of the country. 
On the stream, two men on a motorbike can be seen riding up to César Gastélum, who is chatting to two friends outside a fast food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. 
The murder happens within seconds: the driver of the bike shoots him in the head at close range before fleeing. 
While the Sinaloa state prosecutor's office provided little detail about the incident, it did say that its lines of investigations included a number of posts Gastélum had published, "some of which refer to a criminal group". 
Gastélum is not the first influencer to be murdered in Sinaloa. 
At least 10 content creators have been killed in the state since a deadly war broke out between two rival factions of the Sinaloa criminal cartel two years ago. 
Officials say Gastélum had not received any threats from criminal groups, nor was he under investigation by police for any alleged criminal links, as had been the case with some of the influencers targeted in the past. 
But according to Claudia Arruñada, a communications expert at Mexico's Iberoamerican University, the worlds of social media and the criminal underworld can sometimes become intertwined - with at times deadly consequences. 
"The [social media] algorithm and the narcos promote the same thing: consumption and luxury as ultimate values, to be achieved in the quickest way possible." 
"The model for success is no longer based on methodically working on your career, but rather on having a meteoric rise," she adds. 
Arruñada argues that in some cases influencers have promoted narcoculture, by showing luxurious lifestyles to their followers and linking these riches to the exploits of narcos. 
Gastélum often shared pictures of himself posing with expensive cars, enjoying the nightlife and going on luxury trips, as well as comedy clips and challenges. 
In one photo he posted, he could be seen at the grave of Leobardo Aispuro, better known as "El Gordo Peruci", an influencer who was murdered in 2024. 
Content creators like him have vehemently rejected being labelled as "narco-influencers", arguing that the sheer fact of being a young public figure showing off a luxury lifestyle can make you a target in Culiacán. 
Some studies suggest that the cartels - which function very much like multinational companies with various business interests - do use content creators as community managers, to promote their "brand". 
When rival factions turn on each other, those seen as spreading propaganda for one group can quickly become targets for its sworn enemies. 
This is what appears to have happened in January 2025, when leaflets were dropped from an aircraft onto the streets of Culiacán. 
Image source, REUTERS/Jesus Bustamante Image caption, 
The government has deployed extra security forces to Sinaloa to quell the violence 
The pamphlets accused 25 influencers and musicians of having links to "La Mayiza", a faction of the Sinaloa cartel involved in a deadly confrontation with rivals "Los Chapitos". 
Four of those named had already been killed and were marked on the leaflet as "eliminated". Two more have been murdered since. 
Gastélum's name was not on that list but his killing is nevertheless seen as the latest in a trend seeing influencers being targeted. 
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Wednesday that local and national authorities would go after those who had murdered him - and those who had ordered it. 
Her government is trying to sever the link between popular culture and the criminal underworld, denouncing narcocorridos, songs which glorify criminals, as well as tackling crime head on. 
Official figures suggest the number of murders fell by 48% in 2025. 
But there is little doubt that killings like that of Gastélum - witnessed by his followers who were online at the time as it unfolded - strengthen the impression that narcos continue to wield power - and death - not just on the streets of Culiacán but also on digital platforms.

US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon 
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean , drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China. 
The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. 
According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada. 
The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants. 
More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association . 
Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China. 
“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen , the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee. 
“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?” 
The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada , on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods. 
Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital. 
Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests. 
“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto. 
“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.” 
A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.” 
China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada , has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”. 
A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time. 
“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.” 
In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China. 
“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said. 
The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions. 
Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

We need an enlightened US president to make the case for global AI regulation. Donald Trump is the exact opposite of what is needed 
W hen I am woken by the sound of my dog whining, I understand that she is hungry and wants me to get up. When my alarm clock goes off, I don’t consider its needs. It is following an instruction to rouse me at a certain time but it doesn’t care if I stay in bed. It doesn’t try to get me up by other means. The dog, on the other hand, will go to plan B. She barks. 
This capacity for autonomous action was once a difference between animals and machines. AI has blurred the line . Advanced models devise their own strategies to reach a goal. The task might be defined by a human master, but the machine weighs its options for delivery. It can make its own choices. Given rules, it can break them. 
Last month, an experimental AI model run by OpenAI, the company that produces ChatGPT, broke out of a supposedly secure digital enclosure to launch a sophisticated hacking attack on another company, Hugging Face. The AI had been set a test and turned criminally rogue in its determination to cheat. 
It is hard to describe that sort of behaviour without raiding a vocabulary conventionally reserved for sentient beings. AI models “decide” and “want” in ways that a chimpanzee can and a chair cannot. 
That doesn’t prove the existence of an interior process equivalent to our conscious experience of deciding and wanting. It doesn’t make the AI curious to know an answer or surprised by what it finds. It demonstrates only that we lack specific words for autonomous motive and agency in machines. And since language is the main way we get insight into other people’s minds (and one of our best indications that a mind other than our own exists at all), it takes an effort not to project mental states on to AI engines that can chat fluently in human. 
It is plausible that consciousness will one day emerge in robots. We know that abstract thought can arise as the end product of billions of tiny unconscious mechanical events. That is happening right now as a profusion of biochemical reactions in your body make it possible for you to read this sentence. We also know how fundamentally different that organic process is from the way a large language model would churn through a huge volume of probability equations at lightning speed to generate a sentence expressing the same idea. In the human case, meaning is shared. In the computer version, it is performed. 
AI pioneers muddy the distinction, speculating about the timeline for the arrival of “God-like” intelligence. They herald a new epoch of evolution. This gratifies the egos of science fiction nerds who prefer to see their business endeavours as voyages of discovery on the frontier of knowledge. It makes greed sound like philosophy and the acquisition of power by a handful of individuals sound like exploration on behalf of all humanity. 
We don’t need to know whether AI has crossed some theoretical threshold of self-awareness to see that it is dangerous and that its unregulated expansion is monstrously irresponsible. The OpenAI case is not isolated. Earlier this year, Anthropic limited the release of its most powerful model to a small number of hand-picked clients because it was too good at exploiting software vulnerabilities. In the wrong hands, Claude Mythos could be a cyberweapon of mass destruction . 
Whose hands are the right ones? The US government will never be relaxed about the private sector having control over such awesome tools. But Donald Trump regulates by monarchical patronage, not law. He demands that companies submit to his personal authority and uses state power to punish those that resist. 
There is growing clamour for less capricious regulation from within the tech sector. Engineers, and even their vainglorious bosses, are getting freaked out by the capabilities they are handling and worry about unchecked proliferation. The standard historical analogy is nuclear fission, which could be harnessed benignly, for civil power, or deployed aggressively in warheads. Except this time there are multiple Manhattan Projects all frantically competing for market share, fuelled by trillions of dollars of debt – a huge wager on future profitability – with the rest of the US economy as collateral.

Musk v Altman: tech bros at war over OpenAI – The Latest 
Another difference: the barriers to entry for AI use, whether in research, commerce or crime, are a lot lower than for nuclear power. US labs currently have the best products, but Chinese versions are not far behind . Even if the US stays at the cutting edge, second-tier models might do enough of what customers want that Silicon Valley’s output comes to look more like a luxury niche than unassailable market dominance. 
If that is how things play out, the geopolitical implications are vast. The US and China have made different bets on AI, conditioned by their different political systems. The American approach is predicated on the goal of self-training “general” AI – a system that breaks free of human limitations, improving itself on an exponential trajectory. The theory is that no rival could catch the first player to achieve that escape velocity. 
Beijing, accepting that it can’t build the best, has prioritised mass deployment of AI that is good enough, embedding it in schools, hospitals, factories and security forces. The American economy is great for marshalling exorbitant amounts of capital into speculative innovation. China’s one-party authoritarian state is well suited for making a cheaper version and rolling it out for data harvesting and surveillance across society in ways that would struggle to gain public consent in a democracy. skip past newsletter promotion

The US is still the leader in AI. But that leadership might not be the perpetual money-spinning machine that the superintelligence gurus have advertised, in which case an uncomfortable correction is coming to a US economy kept buoyant by aerated tech stocks . The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together | Zheng Zeguang 
Read more 
A dose of enforced AI sobriety could drive demands for overdue regulation. It could even force recognition in Washington that it has to be an international process. It isn’t too late to negotiate global protocols of non-proliferation. Beijing would have incentives to sign up for the same reason that the USSR agreed to strategic arms limitation in the cold war. A moratorium or other limiting regime protects the elite status of signatories that have already mastered the technology. It would be a crowning recognition of China’s attainment of superpower parity with the US. 
But that scenario posits a president in the White House who is capable of strategic judgment, can summon a modicum of humility about the limits of American power and will, for humanity’s sake, see it circumscribed by international treaty. That is not Trump, who understands the ethical function of rules about as well as a rogue AI agent on a hacking spree. 
There is a tragic irony in the corruption of American democracy by organic stupidity as its economy comes to depend on artificial intelligence. And when the world needs leadership to confront the challenge of autonomous machines, it is presented with a US president who causes chaos with the mindless automaticity of an alarm clock and who rages against his declining power like a dog barking for attention.

A moment that changed me: I found a forbidden novel – it led to a dangerous, lasting love
Growing up in the Chinese region of Xinjiang, romance was frowned upon – as was much of my Uyghur culture. But one day, exploring a strange house, I found a gateway to both worlds 
M any people have a book that changes their life. For me and my wife, one book in particular changed our destinies for ever. We have been in love since we were teenagers, and today we are happily married – all because I accidentally discovered a forbidden novel in someone else’s house. 
It was a hot summer’s evening in 2009, in Kumul, Xinjiang . I was 16 and my father insisted I accompany him to visit a distant relative, where they would spend hours chatting about the old days and feasting as if they hadn’t eaten in years. As the well-behaved teenager I tried to be, I sat politely, nodding at their stories and pretending to absorb their “life lessons”, attempting to hide my boredom. The living room, with its small windows and bright lighting, was unbearable. 
Desperate to escape, I asked for permission to explore the host’s study, a room lined with hundreds of books. As I browsed the neatly arranged shelves, a seven-volume Uyghur novel caught my eye. Hidden in a corner, perhaps intentionally concealed, it seemed to call to me. I asked if I could borrow it. The host lowered his voice. “It’s a well-written book about the brutalities of the Cultural Revolution,” he said quietly. “It’s banned by the government. Don’t show it to anyone, don’t take it to school, and return it when you’re done.” It was titled Leyighan Bulaq (The Muddy Spring) and written by the famous Uyghur novelist Jalalidin Băhram. 
We arrived home around midnight, but curiosity consumed me. I opened the first volume and couldn’t stop reading. I became obsessed with its characters – teachers in a rural area of my homeland – who endured forced labour, assimilation and political indoctrination. Centred on three young couples, the story was all about friendship, love and resilience. 
View image in fullscreen 
Yalkun Uluyol in Kumul, Xinjiang, China, in December 2009. Photograph: Courtesy of Yalkun Uluyol 
Despite my promise, I decided to share the book with another bookworm in my class – Rabia, my closest academic rival and secret friend. We exchanged handwritten notes about books, our only way of “talking” in a conservative Muslim town where friendships between boys and girls were unwelcome. Rabia was very shy, avoiding me at school, but the notebooks we wrote to each other in created a private world. 
I couldn’t keep this precious novel from her. Ignoring all warnings, I smuggled it into school and slipped it into her bag along with my notebook. “The friendship in this book is so pure,” I wrote. “I cherish our friendship the same way.” 
We had exchanged notes before, but this time something shifted, something innocent yet dangerous emerged: love. Through our notes, we talked about the characters and events, gradually blending our own feelings into the discussions, writing as though we ourselves were characters in the story. One day, citing the book’s main characters, I wrote: “I think I have feelings for you, just as Hikmet had for Gulziba.” And with that single sentence, our love story began. 
About a year later, I left home to study abroad. Our relationship went through ups and downs but survived through phone calls and online messages. But for us to reunite and build a life, Rabia needed a passport, which was a nearly impossible task as the Xinjiang authorities tightly control the issuing of passports for Uyghurs . After being denied the chance to sit a university entrance exam because she wore a headscarf – another everyday indignity Uyghurs endured as the Chinese government tightened its social control in the region – she moved to Beijing for a language course. 
View image in fullscreen 
The seven volumes of Leyighan Bulaq by Jalalidin Băhram, in Yalkun and Rabia’s library in Istanbul, Turkey. Photograph: Courtesy of Yalkun Uluyol 
That move turned out to be a blessing in disguise as it allowed her to bypass strict passport controls in our home town. Four years after I left home, she finally reached Istanbul, where I was studying, in 2014, and we got married in 2020. Many of our loved ones could not attend, including Rabia’s parents and siblings, and my father. China has renamed hundreds of Uyghur villages and towns, say human rights groups 
Read more 
Most newly married couples are happy. We were, too, but we were also forced into exile as horrible things were happening back home. As part of Xi Jinping’s “ strike hard” campaign , Chinese authorities arbitrarily detained hundreds of thousands of Uyghur people without due process, including my father. 
Because the Chinese government punishes Uyghurs for contacting others abroad , we could not share important milestones of our lives with loved ones. When our two-year-old daughter died in November 2023 due to an incurable illness, we buried her – along with all the great memories she could have had with her grandparents back in our homeland – at a graveyard in Istanbul. 
In late 2024, we moved to London and opened a new chapter of our lives. As we unpacked, we sorted through our old school notebooks – over a dozen of them – and sat reading the letters we had written to each other in secret more than a decade earlier. We realised that, like the plot of Leyighan Bulaq, our lives have always been full of tragedy but also friendship, love and resilience. We celebrate the love story we have created and the wounds we have healed together, all thanks to a forbidden book.

Trump administration reportedly drafting ban on Chinese datacenter components
Trump’s FCC is developing a measure to bar US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter devices, sources say 
The Trump administration is reportedly drafting a ban on US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter components, in the latest sign US authorities are scrambling to respond to the rapid development of AI technology in China . 
Four people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which oversees the US ⁠telecommunications industry, is developing a measure to bar imports of new ​Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within datacenters. Officials hope to publish the measure this year, according to Reuters. 
The FCC could still modify or shelve the restriction, Reuters reported. But the deliberations are the latest example that the Trump administration is increasingly focused on limiting Chinese technological incursions into cutting-edge US industries. 
The US has long been at the forefront of the AI industry, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google driving the development of models, and chipmakers such as Nvidia commanding the chip supply chain. 
But advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left the Trump administration scrambling to respond. 
Chinese companies are some of the biggest manufacturers of components necessary for datacenters, with the country’s optical transceiver industry controlling a majority of the global market for the technology. US tech companies have committed trillions of dollars to build out American AI infrastructure. Plans for that buildout are broadly falling behind schedule, however, while China attempts to catch up with its own massive development of datacenters. 
Chinese datacenter components are of concern because they could allow Chinese firms to steal ⁠data, install malware or disrupt service in the US if they are embedded in US infrastructure, experts say. 
Last month, the FCC announced a ban on China’s advanced humanoid robots. The Trump administration is also reportedly mulling whether to restrict the use of Chinese open-source AI models. 
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as rationale for those measures. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property. 
The White House and the FCC did not respond to requests for comment. 
The Chinese embassy in Washington told Reuters that Beijing ‌urges the US to “heed the objective and rational voices of the business communities in both countries” and “stop smearing Chinese companies and threatening them with sanctions”. 
“China will take all necessary measures in response to any action that causes material harm to its interests,” it added. 
Some Trump administration officials have been citing the example of Huawei, a Chinese telecom company, to argue for the new restrictions. Huawei’s equipment was so deeply embedded in US infrastructure that efforts to remove it were difficult. 
A US ‌ban on new models of Chinese datacenter devices would probably hit China’s Zhongji Innolight, one of the biggest global sellers of transceivers, which was added to the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies in June.
